//go:build integration

package integration

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"strings"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/agent/types"
	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/proclive"
	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/session"
	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/strategy"
	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/testutil"
	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
)

func TestStatusMultipleSessionsPreservedAcrossWorktrees(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()
	env := NewRepoWithCommit(t)
	env.RunCLI("enable", "--agent", agentClaudeCode, "--telemetry=false")
	linked := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "linked")
	testutil.RunGit(t, env.RepoDir, "worktree", "add", "-b", "status-linked", linked)

	store := session.NewStateStoreWithDir(filepath.Join(env.RepoDir, ".git", session.SessionStateDirName))
	lastActive := time.Now().UTC().Add(-time.Minute)
	for _, state := range []*session.State{
		{SessionID: "same-agent-main", WorktreeID: "main", WorktreePath: env.RepoDir, Branch: "main", StartedAt: lastActive.Add(-time.Hour), LastInteractionTime: &lastActive, Phase: session.PhaseActive, AgentType: types.AgentType(agentClaudeCode)},
		{SessionID: "same-agent-linked", WorktreeID: "linked", WorktreePath: linked, Branch: "status-linked", StartedAt: lastActive.Add(-2 * time.Hour), LastInteractionTime: &lastActive, Phase: session.PhaseActive, AgentType: types.AgentType(agentClaudeCode)},
	} {
		require.NoError(t, store.Save(t.Context(), state))
	}

	var got struct {
		ActiveSessions []struct {
			SessionID    string `json:"session_id"`
			WorktreePath string `json:"worktree_path"`
		} `json:"active_sessions"`
	}
	require.NoError(t, json.Unmarshal([]byte(env.RunCLI("status", "--json")), &got))
	require.Len(t, got.ActiveSessions, 2)
	require.Equal(t, []string{"same-agent-linked", "same-agent-main"}, []string{got.ActiveSessions[0].SessionID, got.ActiveSessions[1].SessionID})
	require.ElementsMatch(t, []string{linked, env.RepoDir}, []string{got.ActiveSessions[0].WorktreePath, got.ActiveSessions[1].WorktreePath})
}

func TestStatusReadOnlyPreservesDeadOwnerStateAndTranscript(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()
	env := NewRepoWithCommit(t)
	env.RunCLI("enable", "--agent", agentClaudeCode, "--telemetry=false")
	transcriptPath := filepath.Join(env.RepoDir, "status-read-only.jsonl")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(transcriptPath, []byte("unchanged\n"), 0o600))
	store := session.NewStateStoreWithDir(filepath.Join(env.RepoDir, ".git", session.SessionStateDirName))
	lastActive := time.Now().UTC().Add(-time.Minute)
	state := &session.State{
		SessionID: "dead-owner-status", WorktreeID: "main", WorktreePath: env.RepoDir, Branch: "main",
		StartedAt: lastActive.Add(-time.Hour), LastInteractionTime: &lastActive,
		Phase: session.PhaseActive, AgentType: types.AgentType(agentClaudeCode),
		Owner: &proclive.Identity{PID: os.Getpid(), Start: "not-this-process"}, TranscriptPath: transcriptPath,
	}
	require.NoError(t, store.Save(t.Context(), state))
	statePath := filepath.Join(env.RepoDir, ".git", session.SessionStateDirName, state.SessionID+".json")
	beforeState, err := os.ReadFile(statePath)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	beforeStateInfo, err := os.Stat(statePath)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	beforeTranscript, err := os.ReadFile(transcriptPath)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	beforeTranscriptInfo, err := os.Stat(transcriptPath)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	text := env.RunCLI("status")
	jsonStatus := env.RunCLI("status", "--json")
	require.Contains(t, text, "dead-owner-status")
	require.Contains(t, text, "exited")
	require.Contains(t, jsonStatus, `"status":"exited"`)
	afterState, err := os.ReadFile(statePath)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	afterStateInfo, err := os.Stat(statePath)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	afterTranscript, err := os.ReadFile(transcriptPath)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	afterTranscriptInfo, err := os.Stat(transcriptPath)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Equal(t, beforeState, afterState)
	require.Equal(t, beforeStateInfo.ModTime(), afterStateInfo.ModTime())
	require.Equal(t, beforeTranscript, afterTranscript)
	require.Equal(t, beforeTranscriptInfo.ModTime(), afterTranscriptInfo.ModTime())
}

1844:- **Reclaiming sessions whose agent vanished** - not every agent fires a session-end hook, and any agent can be killed before its hook runs, so a session can be left un-finalized forever. `SessionState.Owner` — the same fingerprint commit linking matches above — is captured at every turn start by `captureSessionOwner`, and `State.OwnerExited()` reports it gone via `proclive.Check`. `finalizeExitedSessions` sweeps those inside `entire status` (text and `--json`) and `entire doctor`, ending them exactly as a clean stop would. **`OwnerExited` deliberately covers IDLE as well as ACTIVE** — an agent that finishes its last turn and then quits leaves IDLE, so gating on ACTIVE alone missed the common case; only already-finalized sessions are excluded, per the shared `State.IsEnded()` predicate. Liveness is Unknown on Windows and for cross-host state, where behaviour degrades to the `StuckActiveThreshold` timeout. Because the sweep runs inside interactive commands, its eager condensing is capped by `sweepCondenseBudget` across the whole sweep: every candidate is always marked ENDED (a single atomic rename — that is what un-sticks it from `entire status`), while condensing runs only while the budget lasts, so a multi-day backlog drains over successive invocations instead of stalling one. Skipping a condense is the existing fail-open path — PostCommit retries, and `doctor` reports the session as "ended with uncondensed checkpoint data".

cd /private/tmp/ent-sessions && gh issue create --title "entire status collapses multiple sessions per agent, and mutates session state while reporting it" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Two related problems in how `entire status` reports sessions. Filing them together because one change fixes both, and because each is a deliberate behaviour change worth recording.

## 1. `--json` collapses sessions to one entry per agent

`active_sessions` deduplicates by agent — one entry per agent, with "active" winning over "idle". A developer running two sessions for the same agent (one per worktree, a normal setup) sees only one of them, and the output carries nothing that would let a consumer recover the other.

The text path already lists every session, grouped by worktree, so the two surfaces disagree.

## 2. Reporting mutates what is reported

Both the text and JSON paths read sessions through `StateStore.List`, which deletes stale records as a side effect of reading, and both then run `finalizeExitedSessions`, which ends any session whose agent process has exited.

So running `entire status` — the command people run to look at state — changes that state. A stale session disappears because you looked at it, and a dead-owner session is finalized on read rather than being reported as exited.

## Desired behaviour

- one entry per session, carrying enough metadata (`session_id`, `worktree_path`, `branch`) to tell two sessions for the same agent apart
- status reads read-only and finalizes nothing; a dead-owner session is reported as `exited` and left alone
- cleanup stays with the callers that own it: `entire doctor` and the session sweeper

## Note for consumers

This changes the `active_sessions` JSON shape from one entry per agent to one entry per session. Consumers that group on the `agent` field keep working; anything relying on exactly one entry per agent does not. The reverse was not possible before — a collapsed entry could not be un-collapsed.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

## Problem

`entire status` had two defects in how it reports sessions, both fixed here.

**`--json` collapsed `active_sessions` to one entry per agent.** Two sessions for the same agent — one per worktree, a normal setup — showed as one, and nothing in the output let a consumer recover the second. The text path already listed every session, so the two surfaces disagreed.

**Reporting mutated what it reported.** Both paths read through `StateStore.List`, which deletes stale records as it reads, and both ran `finalizeExitedSessions`. Running the command people run to *look* at state changed that state: a stale session vanished because you looked at it, and a dead-owner session was finalized on read instead of being reported as exited.

## Summary

- add `StateStore.ListReadOnly` beside the existing mutating reads, splitting stale cleanup behind a parameter
- status reads read-only on both the text and JSON paths and finalizes nothing
- `--json` reports one entry per session, carrying `session_id`, `worktree_path`, and `branch`

`List` and `Load` keep their cleanup contract exactly as before — `entire doctor` and the session sweeper still call them and still finalize, verified by test.

def cut(src, name):
    """Remove a top-level test function by name."""
    m=re.search(r'(?:^//[^\n]*\n)*^func '+re.escape(name)+r'\(t \*testing\.T\) \{', src, re.M)
    if not m: return src, False
    start=m.start()
    nxt=re.search(r'\n(?=func )', src[m.end():])

cd /private/tmp/ent-hooks && git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
fix(hooks): recognize Lefthook launchers structurally, not byte-exactly

looksLikeLefthookHook matched Lefthook's generated wrapper body byte for
byte, pinning every package-manager probe branch it ships with — mise,
devbox, uv, bundle, yarn, pnpm, mint, go tool. The next Lefthook release
changes that body, at which point the check returns false,
inspectActiveHookDelivery reports the bridge absent, and Entire writes native
wrappers over Lefthook's own hooks. That is #1349 in reverse, triggered by a
routine upgrade, with no error and no test that would notice.

Its sibling knownDirectEntireLefthookBody was worse in kind: the two strings
it matched were byte-identical to fixtures written by this repo's own
integration and e2e tests. Shipping code had been extended to recognize test
doubles, which meant no test exercised the branch real Lefthook takes.

Replace both with lefthookBodyDispatches. Structure alone will not do — a
no-op wrapper carries the same preamble and dispatch line, and accepting it
would report healthy delivery while no hook runs. A bare substring will not
either: the word appears in paths (.lefthook-local/<hook>/entire.sh
dispatches to Entire) and in messages (Lefthook's own fallback ends
`echo "Can't find lefthook in PATH"`). So drop quoted literals containing
whitespace, then require a word whose basename is the binary.

Validated against the real lefthook 2.1.10 generated body plus every fixture
in the tree and three adversarial shapes.

The simulated launchers now dispatch through a shim binary named lefthook
rather than exec'ing entire.sh inline, so they exercise the same path a real
install does instead of a shape only our tests produce.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

The deactivate/finishDeactivation dance is gone with it. It existed to hide
the config while scripts were being written, a window of microseconds in a
file read only when a git hook fires, and config-last closes it by
construction.

| Task | | Production |
| --- | --- | --- |
| — | starting point after PR 1 split out | 2,989 |
| 5 | byte-exact matchers → validated predicate | 2,945 |
| 6 | staging engine → ordered atomic writes | **2,776** |

Both landed with full `strategy` + integration suites and lint green, committed.

**What Task 6 actually removed:** a staging/rollback engine — stage, deactivate, publish, finishDeactivation, roll back — for placing seven small files, nested *inside* `EnsureGitHookIntegration`'s snapshot of the same paths plus the native hooks and backups. Write order is now the transaction: scripts and `info/exclude` first, config last, since the config is what makes Lefthook dispatch.

**One plan defect found and corrected:** Task 6's budget line said to delete `snapshotHookIntegration` too, but Step 2 requires the rollback test to pass *against the outer snapshot alone*. Following the budget would have left no rollback at all. | **8** — hot-path caches | the +121/−9 already written | **+112** |
| | | **net −1,660 → ~1,116** |

**The +112 is my error.** Task 8 *adds* two memoization caches and the `EnsureSetup` gate; I never put it in the target table when I built it from per-file reductions. The table said 950 while the plan simultaneously required a change that adds ~112 lines. So the real target was always ~1,060, not 950.

**The biggest risk is `hook_integration_transaction.go`: 655 → 235.** That's the largest single remaining cut and the least certain, because it depends on three things at once — the removal cluster collapsing (204 → ~105 by reusing `RemoveGitHook` and merging `verifyRemoved`/`AnyInstalled`), `openEffectiveHooksRoot` 53 → ~8, and the per-hook ownership change. If that one lands at 300 instead of 235, the total is ~1,180.

So: **expect ~1,100, with ~1,050–1,200 the honest range.** Against 3,156 today that's still a ~65% cut in production code, and against the original 6,807-line PR it's the difference between one unreviewable diff and two reviewable ones.

Two options if you want it genuinely under 1,000:

1. **Drop the hot-path fix from PR 2** and ship it as its own ~120-line PR. It's independent of everything else, trivially reviewable on its own, and removes the +112. That gets PR 2 to ~1,000 without giving anything up.

in precedence order, and a non-YAML local config is refused rather than
shadowed — writing into a shadowed file would be a silent no-op.

cd /private/tmp/ent-hooks && gh pr create --draft --base main --head fix/lefthook-durable-hooks --title "fix(hooks): keep checkpoint delivery working when Lefthook reclaims hooks" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
**Draft — Tasks 8–12 of the rework still to come.** Opening it now so the work is visible rather than sitting on a local branch.

Replaces the implementation in #2343, which bundled this with an unrelated session-listing change (now #2363) and carried a lot of machinery this drops.

## Problem

In a repo that also uses Lefthook, Lefthook reclaims Entire's Git hooks — on any `lefthook.yml` edit (#1349) or on the `lefthook install -f` that its npm postinstall runs (#2263). Checkpoint capture and delivery then stop silently, and `entire status` reports nothing wrong (#2264).

## Approach

Entire owns `entire-lefthook.yml` outright and adds exactly one `extends` entry to the local config. Lefthook resolves `extends` at run time, so an already-installed launcher dispatches to Entire's scripts immediately — no `lefthook install`, no user action — and the main config is never read, so its format stops mattering.

Verified end to end against the real lefthook 2.1.10 binary with a **`lefthook.toml`** main config, a layout the previous mechanism refused outright: `enable` writes both artifacts, the team config keeps zero Entire references, status reports `mode=lefthook state=current`, and after `lefthook install -f` strips every native hook a commit still lands a checkpoint and a push still delivers it.

## What this drops from #2343

- **Byte-exact matching of Lefthook's generated wrapper body.** It pinned every package-manager probe branch, so the next Lefthook release would read as a foreign hook — and Entire would then write native wrappers over Lefthook's own hooks, which is #1349 in reverse. Its sibling matched two strings byte-identical to this repo's own test fixtures, so no test exercised the branch real Lefthook takes.
- **A second, nested rollback layer.** `installLefthookFilesAt` staged and rolled back files that `EnsureGitHookIntegration` had already snapshotted, along with the native hooks and their backups. Write order is the transaction now: scripts first, the activating entry last.
- **The merge into the user's `lefthook-local.yml`** — `source_dir_local` plus a nested scripts entry per hook — and with it `validateLefthookMainConfig`, the main-config-derived rejections, and eight near-identical `yaml.Node` traversals. `lefthook_yaml.go` is gone.

## Coverage goes up

`lefthook.toml`, `lefthook.jsonc`, `.config/lefthook.yml`, and repos using `extends` or `remotes` previously degraded to the native bridge, which Lefthook then clobbered. They now work. The test that pinned them as unsupported asserts the opposite.

## Known issue, not introduced here

The generated pre-push script passes `"$2"` unconditionally, so hooks written by this version fail against an older `entire` on `PATH` (`accepts 1 arg(s), received 2`). The ABI widening came from #2343; flagging it because it is a real mixed-version hazard and is currently undocumented.

## Still to do

- turn-start latency fix (measured 25.3ms → 197µs on `CheckGitHookIntegration`; `EnsureSetup` lost its already-installed gate on main)
- move hook-health warnings from stdout to stderr, dropping the claim/hint/rollback protocol
- test consolidation, docs, rebase onto current main

Closes #2264, #1349, #2263 when complete. Does **not** close #2237 — that backup-chain path is untouched here.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

Here's the arithmetic. To hit 2,500 total I need tests at ~1,200 (from 3,340) with production at ~1,150. Planned trimming gets tests to ~2,430. **Trimming can't close it — it needs a scope cut.**

The clean one: **drop the proactive warnings from PR 2.**

| | Production | Tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `strategy/session_state.go` | 240 | 166 |
| `lifecycle.go` | 210 | 268 |
| `agent/agent.go` + `geminicli` | 28 | — |
| integration warning tests | — | ~30 |
| **Removed** | **−478** | **−464** |

That's the whole warning subsystem gone rather than rewritten to stderr — and it's defensible on its own terms, not just as line-cutting:

- **It was never part of #2264, #1349, or #2263.** Those are "status lies," "Lefthook clobbers hooks," and "wrong warning text." Proactively notifying agents mid-turn is a separate feature, and **#1965 is the open issue that actually asks for it.**
- It was scope creep in #2343 — the checkpoint record shows it was requested mid-session, not filed.
- PR 2 still closes all three of its issues without it: hooks survive Lefthook, and `entire status` plus `entire doctor` both report health truthfully.

Combined with real test consolidation — `hook_integration_test.go` 977 → ~400, and merging the two `lefthook_integration*_test.go` files (283 + 274) → ~350:

| | Lines |
| --- | --- |
| Production | ~740 |
| Tests | ~1,650 |
| Docs + e2e | ~155 |
| **Total** | **~2,545** |

That lands the agreement, and production comes in *under* the 950 figure too.

What you give up: users don't get told their hooks are broken until they run `status` or `doctor`. That's exactly the gap #1965 describes, and it becomes that issue's PR — roughly 40 lines on stderr, as the plan already worked out.

Want me to take that route? It means reverting the warning code out of PR 2 rather than rewriting it, which is less work than Task 9 as planned.

Good question to force, and the numbers give a clear answer.

**PR 2 is 93% additive**: +2,047 production, **−144**. It doesn't remove broken code — it adds a second mechanism beside the existing one.

**What's actually broken today**, precisely:

1. Entire installs native hooks into `.git/hooks/*`.
2. Lefthook's `install -f` — which its npm postinstall runs on *every* `npm install` — rewrites those files. Entire's hooks are gone, silently. Same for any `lefthook.yml` edit (#1349).
3. **But main already self-heals.** `EnsureSetup` runs at every agent turn start:
   ```go
   if !IsGitHookInstalled(ctx) {
       if _, err := ReinstallGitHooks(ctx); err != nil {
   ```

**How the conflict arises**

1. lefthook installs and manages `pre-push`. Its installed hooks self-sync on every run, gated by a checksum of `lefthook.yml` stored in `.git/info/lefthook.checksum`.
2. `entire enable` / `entire configure --force` wraps the existing hook: it renames the current `pre-push` to `pre-push.pre-entire` and installs its own wrapper that runs the entire handler then chains down:
   ```sh
   # Entire CLI hooks
   if command -v entire >/dev/null 2>&1; then entire hooks git pre-push "$1" || true; else :; fi
   # Chain: run pre-existing hook
   "$(dirname "$0")/pre-push.pre-entire" "$@"
   ```
   At this point both run on push — entire pushes session logs, then chains to lefthook. 👍
3. **But** whenever `lefthook.yml` changes, lefthook's checksum goes stale. Its next self-sync (at the top of any lefthook-managed hook, e.g. the next commit's `pre-commit`) sees that `pre-push` is no longer *its* hook, backs entire's wrapper up to `pre-push.old`, and reinstalls its own bare hook. **entire's session push is now silently gone.**
4. On the next `lefthook.yml` change after that, lefthook also emits a recurring warning, because its earlier backup collides:
   ```
   sync hooks: ❌
   could not replace the hook: can't rename pre-push to pre-push.old - file already exists
   ```

**Why there is no clean user-side fix** (verified on 0.7.3)

I got that wrong, and it matters. Re-reading #1349:

> Its next self-sync (**at the top of any lefthook-managed hook, e.g. the next commit's `pre-commit`**) sees that `pre-push` is no longer *its* hook, backs entire's wrapper up to `pre-push.old`, and reinstalls its own bare hook.

So the sequence is:

1. Agent turn starts → `EnsureSetup` reinstalls Entire's hooks ✓
2. Agent commits → **lefthook's `pre-commit` fires and reclaims `pre-push` during that commit**
3. Push → Entire's pre-push is gone → checkpoints silently not delivered

**The turn-start self-heal cannot cover this**, because the clobber is triggered *by the commit itself*, after the heal already ran. My "window between npm install and the next agent turn" was wrong — there is no window to miss. It re-breaks on every commit once the checksum is stale.

Triggers, both routine:
- **any `lefthook.yml` edit** — including pulling a teammate's change (#1349)
- **any `npm install`**, via lefthook's postinstall running `install -f` (#2263)

And the reporter had already tested the cheap fix and ruled it out: *"The only local mitigation is a self-heal step that re-wraps after each re-sync, which still can't cover a push that happens with no intervening commit."* There's also a secondary failure — once `pre-push.old` exists, lefthook starts erroring on every subsequent sync.

So: in a repo using both tools, checkpoint delivery is broken **continuously** after any config change, not in a narrow gap. That's the ticket's actual scenario, and it's why becoming a Lefthook-native citizen — no file for lefthook to reclaim — is the right mechanism rather than more self-healing.

I nearly argued you out of the fix on a misreading, and floated a ~250-line alternative that would have left #1349 unfixed while status truthfully reported "blocked" forever. Withdraw that. The ~2,000 lines are buying a real, continuous, silent data-loss bug — that's proportionate.

content.text:
You're right, and that's the actual architectural smell in this PR — I flagged it as "Task 6 Step 4" and then never did it.

Here's what `EnsureGitHookIntegration` does in a Lefthook repo today:

```go
// 1. install Entire's lefthook artifacts
activeCurrent, err := inspectActiveHookDelivery(ctx, repoRoot)
if !activeCurrent {
    nativeWritten, installErr := InstallGitHook(ctx, true, absolutePath)  // 2. ALSO write native hooks
}
if err := restoreProvenLefthookBridges(ctx, absolutePath); err != nil {   // 3. undo some of step 2
```

It installs the Lefthook integration, **then writes native hooks on top**, then walks back and un-writes the ones that were Lefthook launchers. Two mechanisms running at once, reconciled at runtime. That's the second layer.

**Repairing the failure means owning nothing Lefthook can reclaim.** The failure is that Entire's wrapper sits in `.git/hooks/pre-push`, Lefthook's checksum sync sees a file that isn't its own, and replaces it. If Entire never writes that file in a Lefthook-managed repo, there is nothing to reclaim and nothing to heal.

So it should be one mechanism chosen by repo state, not two layered:

- **Lefthook config present *and* Lefthook's launchers installed** → Entire registers via `extends` and touches no file in `.git/hooks`
- **anything else** (no Lefthook, or Lefthook configured but never `install`ed) → Entire's ordinary native hooks, exactly as on main

The "bridge" case isn't a bridge at all — it's just "Lefthook isn't actually managing hooks here," where native hooks were never at risk.

What that deletes:

| | Lines |
| --- | --- |
| `restoreProvenLefthookBridges` | 60 |
| `inspectActiveHookDelivery` | 22 |
| `looksLikeLefthookHook` + `lefthookBodyDispatches` | 49 |
| native-hook entries in the snapshot/restore | ~15 |
| `hook_integration.go`'s `lefthook_native_bridge` degraded states | ~40 |
| their tests | ~200 |

**~185 production, ~200 tests**, and — more to your point — it removes the entire class of "which of our two mechanisms is live right now" reasoning, including the byte-matching of Lefthook's wrapper that caused the defect I fixed in Task 5. If Entire never inspects or writes those files, it never needs to recognize them.

It also means the answer to "is delivery working?" becomes one question per mode instead of a matrix.

Want me to make that change? It's the right fix and it's a net simplification, but it's a real behavioural decision: in a Lefthook repo, Entire would stop installing native hooks entirely, so a user who removes Lefthook would need an `entire enable` to get native hooks back.

Facts from the code:

| Manager | `OverwritesHooks` | Integration kind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Husky** | `true` | `hookDirectory` |
| **Lefthook** | `true` (set by this PR) | `lefthook` |

So it isn't only Lefthook — **Husky clobbers too, and Entire already knows.** But Husky has a real fix and Lefthook doesn't, for three reasons that compound:

1. **Where the hooks live.** Husky sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/` and puts hook scripts there. Entire isn't in direct contention for `.git/hooks/*`. Lefthook writes straight into `.git/hooks/*` — the same files Entire wants.

2. **When it reclaims.** This is the real differentiator. From #1349: Lefthook's *installed hooks self-sync on every run*, gated by a `lefthook.yml` checksum. So it re-claims **from inside a hook Entire didn't install, during a normal commit** — not just at `lefthook install` time. Husky overwrites on `npm install`; Lefthook overwrites continuously. That's why self-healing at turn start loses to Lefthook but would be adequate for Husky.

3. **Whether a permanent user-side fix exists.** Husky's hook files are *committed*, so Entire's advice — "add these lines to your `.husky` hook files" — sticks, and that's the `hookDirectory` branch you can see in `hookManagerWarning`. Lefthook's hook files are *generated from config*, so there's no file to edit. That's precisely #2263's complaint: flipping Lefthook's flag alone produces advice that reads `lefthook.ymlpre-push:`, because the `true` branch assumes `ConfigPath` is a directory.

So Lefthook is the one manager that owns the contended files, regenerates them continuously, and offers the user nothing to edit. Hence a config-level integration rather than a warning or a self-heal.

**One thing I'd flag as unverified:** `pre-commit`, `Overcommit`, and `hk` are classified `false` on the current code's say-so. #2263 demonstrated that Lefthook's `false` was simply wrong, and nobody has re-tested the other three the same way. `pre-commit install --overwrite` and `overcommit --install` both rewrite `.git/hooks/*`, so at least one of those classifications is worth checking — but that's a separate issue, not this PR.

content.text:
Same *pattern*, different *execution* — and that difference is worth naming precisely.

**Husky today:** Entire detects it, prints a warning, and tells the user *"add these lines to your `.husky` hook files."* The user edits files they own and commit. Entire writes nothing. Advisory.

**Lefthook in this PR:** Entire writes its own config file and registers itself. No user action. Automatic.

So it's the pattern the codebase already treats as correct — integrate at the manager's config level instead of fighting for `.git/hooks/*` — but applied automatically rather than as instructions.

And that exposes a smaller option I should have put on the table:

**#2263's literal ask is the advisory version.** Quoting it:

> `true`: **"Warning: X detected"**, plus the exact lines to add to X's own hook files so Entire survives permanently.

For Lefthook that's a `scripts:` entry the user adds to their committed `lefthook.yml`. That's maybe **50 lines** — reclassify Lefthook, fix the advice branch so it emits a scripts entry instead of `lefthook.ymlpre-push:`, done. It even has an advantage over what we built: committed to `lefthook.yml`, it's team-wide, where our `lefthook-local.yml` entry is per-clone.

What it doesn't do is **#1349**, which asks for the problem to stop happening rather than be documented. Its four proposed fixes are manager-aware install, decouple handler from ownership, register via the host manager, or self-repair. This PR implements option 3 automatically.

So the honest framing of the choice:

| | Lines | Closes | Requires |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Advisory (Husky-style) | ~50 + ~215 for status truth | #2263, #2264 | every user to act, per repo |
| Automatic (`extends`) | ~2,000 | #2263, #2264, **#1349** | nothing |

I've been building the second without ever putting the first in front of you, and "it's what we already do for Husky" is a fair reason to ask why. The real argument for automatic is that Lefthook re-breaks on every commit after a config change — so advisory means every developer on the team has to have acted, in advance, or they silently lose checkpoints. But that's an argument to weigh, not one I should have assumed.

content.text:
The root-cause fix *is* general — it's the registration mechanism that can't be.

The general principle: **git gives one file per hook, so only one tool can own it. The other has to register with the owner.** That resolves the conflict for any manager, and it's what this does.

But "register with the owner" has no common implementation:

| Manager | Registration point |
| --- | --- |
| Lefthook | config file; `scripts:`/`commands:` entries; supports `extends` and a local variant |
| Husky | `.husky/<hook>` shell files, committed to the repo |
| pre-commit | `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `repo: local` entries |
| Overcommit | `.overcommit.yml` hook definitions, plus its signature system |
| hk | `hk.pkl` |

Different formats, different ownership markers, different removal, different "is it still installed" checks. A general fix is an interface plus N adapters — **more** code than one adapter, not less. The interface is maybe 50 lines; each adapter is a few hundred.

And there's no manager-agnostic escape hatch. `core.hooksPath` is the obvious candidate, but it's a single value and Husky already claims it — two tools can't both redirect it.

So the sequencing argument: build the first adapter properly, and #1250 ("external Git hooks backend for Rush, Husky, and others") becomes "add the second," at which point the shared shape is visible from two real examples instead of guessed from one.

**Where I'd agree the current code is dishonest about this:** it already carries a `hookManagerIntegrationKind` enum with three values, which *looks* like the abstraction but isn't one — there's no `hookBackend` interface, and `CheckGitHookIntegration` and `EnsureGitHookIntegration` are both `if lefthook { …110 lines… }` inline. So it pays for the concept of a general backend while giving #1250 nothing. That enum should be a plain `bool` or a name comparison until there's a second adapter to design against.

The other thing worth doing now, cheaply: **verify the other classifications.** `pre-commit`, `Overcommit`, and `hk` are marked as not-overwriting on the current code's say-so, and #2263 proved that exact claim was wrong for Lefthook. `pre-commit install --overwrite` and `overcommit --install` both rewrite `.git/hooks/*`. If one of them also reclaims continuously, it needs the same treatment, and we'd know whether the adapter shape generalizes before committing to it.

Want me to test those three the way I tested Lefthook? It's maybe twenty minutes and it either confirms Lefthook is genuinely the outlier or tells us #1250 is more urgent than it looks.

content.text:
Tested all three the same way I tested Lefthook. Results:

| Manager | Clobbers on `install`? | Reclaims a *different* hook during a commit, after a config change? | Currently flagged |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Lefthook** | yes | **yes** — continuously | `true` (this PR) |
| **pre-commit** | **yes** — warns, backs up to `.legacy` | no | **`false`** ❌ |
| **Overcommit** | **yes** — moves to `.git/hooks/old-hooks` | no | **`false`** ❌ |
| **hk** | **yes** — the hooks it declares | no | **`false`** ❌ |
| Husky | yes (npm install) | not tested — uses `core.hooksPath` | `true` |

**Two conclusions, and they point in opposite directions.**

**1. The `OverwritesHooks` classification is wrong for all three.** Every one of them overwrites Entire's hooks at install time. `pre-commit` even prints *"Use -f to use only pre-commit"* and saves `.pre-commit.legacy`; Overcommit announces *"Hook already exists and was not installed by Overcommit. Moving to old-hooks"*. So users of those three get the weaker "Note:" message today when they should get the warning — the same defect #2263 filed for Lefthook, unfixed for three more managers. That's a small, separate fix.

**2. Lefthook really is the outlier, and that's the load-bearing finding.** It's the only one that reclaims *continuously*. The other three clobber once, at an explicit install the user ran — after which Entire's existing `EnsureSetup` self-heal restores the hooks on the next turn and they stay restored. Lefthook re-breaks on every commit while the checksum is stale, from inside a hook Entire didn't install, so the self-heal never wins.

So the answer to "why not fix it in general": **because the general fix isn't needed.** Three of the four other managers are adequately served by the self-heal that already exists plus a corrected warning — roughly a one-line classification change and the advice-shape fix. Only Lefthook defeats self-healing, and only Lefthook therefore justifies a config-level integration.

That also means #1250's "general backend" would be built for a problem only one manager has. I'd leave it open and not build the abstraction — which supports dropping the `hookManagerIntegrationKind` enum down to a plain check, since there's now evidence rather than a guess that a second adapter isn't imminent.

Worth filing the misclassification as its own issue — it's a real user-facing bug affecting three managers, it's ~20 lines, and it shouldn't ride along in this PR. Want me to write it up?

content.text:
Two questions, both worth being precise about.

## What exactly is misclassified

`detectHookManagers()` in `hook_managers.go` tags each manager with one bool:

```go
{Name: "Husky",      ConfigPath: ".husky/",                OverwritesHooks: true,  ...},
{Name: "pre-commit", ConfigPath: ".pre-commit-config.yaml",                        ...},  // false
{Name: "Overcommit", ConfigPath: ".overcommit.yml",                                ...},  // false
// hk: also false
// Lefthook: false on main; this PR sets it true (that's #2263)
```

That bool picks which message `entire enable` prints:

| flag | message |
| --- | --- |
| `true` | **"Warning: X detected"** + how to survive its reinstalls |
| `false` | "Note: X detected" + "if X reinstalls hooks, run `entire enable`" |

My tests showed pre-commit, Overcommit and hk all *do* overwrite — pre-commit literally prints *"Use -f to use only pre-commit"* and saves `.pre-commit.legacy`; Overcommit prints *"Hook already exists and was not installed by Overcommit. Moving to old-hooks"*. So three managers give the softer "Note:" when the facts say "Warning:".

**The fix is three `OverwritesHooks: true` values** — not 20 lines, more like 3. They're all `IntegrationKind: none`, so they land in the branch that says *"X may overwrite hooks… run `entire enable` to restore"*, which is accurate for them. No new advice code needed.

## Are there two separate issues

Yes, and #2263 conflates them:

- **The mechanism problem** — hooks actually get clobbered. Lefthook does it *continuously* (defeats self-heal → needs the config integration). The other three do it *once, at an explicit install the user ran* (self-heal already covers it).
- **The messaging problem** — Entire tells the user the wrong thing. Wrong flag for three managers, and for Lefthook the `true` branch's advice is malformed because it assumes `ConfigPath` is a directory.

## Where the fix goes

It should ride along in PR 2. Same file (`hook_managers.go`, already +33/−15 there), same function, and PR 2 already closes #2263 — which *is* the classification issue. Splitting a three-value change into its own PR would be worse than the scope creep we've been trimming.

What I'd do: flip the three flags, and add a test pinning each manager's classification with a comment recording how it was verified — so the next person doesn't have to re-derive it from behaviour the way I just did.

Want me to add that to PR 2?

content.text:
Here's the full picture, by scenario.

## 1. Lefthook repo — the case that needs the mechanism

**Today**
1. `entire enable` writes Entire's hooks into `.git/hooks/*`, prints *"Note: Lefthook detected… if Lefthook reinstalls hooks, run `entire enable`"*
2. Someone edits `lefthook.yml` — or any `npm install` runs Lefthook's postinstall — and its checksum goes stale
3. Next `git commit`: Lefthook's own `pre-commit` fires, self-syncs, and **reclaims `pre-push` mid-commit**
4. `git push` → Entire's pre-push is gone → **checkpoints silently not delivered**
5. `entire status` says *"Checkpoints sync to: origin"* — false
6. `entire doctor` says *"Git hooks: NOT INSTALLED"* — the two disagree
7. Next agent turn reinstalls the hooks… and step 3 breaks them again on the next commit

**After PR 2**
1. `entire enable` writes `entire-lefthook.yml`, one `extends` entry, and the scripts. Entire writes **nothing** into `.git/hooks/*`
2. Lefthook regenerates its hooks whenever it likes — there's nothing of Entire's to reclaim
3. Commit → Lefthook's hook → Entire's script → **checkpoint captured**
4. Push → **delivered**
5. `entire status` → `Git hooks · current (lefthook)`, `checkpoint_sync_state: ready`
6. Warning text is correct: *"Warning: Lefthook detected"* with a usable fix

## 2. pre-commit / Overcommit / hk repo

**Today**
1. `entire enable` installs native hooks, prints the soft *"Note: X detected"*
2. User runs `pre-commit install` / `overcommit --install` / `hk install` → **Entire's hooks are clobbered** (backed up to `.legacy` / `old-hooks`)
3. Commits and pushes before the next agent turn aren't captured or delivered
4. `entire status` still says checkpoints sync — false
5. Next agent turn reinstalls, and it **stays** fixed, because these don't reclaim continuously

**After PR 2**
- Step 2's message becomes *"**Warning**: X detected… may overwrite hooks installed by Entire… run `entire enable` to restore"* — the classification fix
- Step 4 becomes `Checkpoint sync blocked … run 'entire doctor'` — the status fix
- **The mechanism is unchanged.** Still native hooks plus the existing self-heal, which my testing showed is adequate for these three

## 3. Husky repo

Unchanged — already flagged `true`, already gets the "add these lines to your `.husky` files" advice, and its committed hook files make that stick.

## 4. No hook manager

Unchanged. Native hooks, nothing to contend with.

---

## Which fix does what

| Fix | Size | Who it helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Lefthook `extends` integration** (#1349) | ~2,000 | Lefthook users only — the sole manager that defeats self-heal |
| **Status reports hook health** (#2264) | ~215 | **Everyone.** Status stops lying whenever hooks are missing, for any cause |
| **Classification fix** (#2263) | ~3 | pre-commit / Overcommit / hk users get the accurate warning |

Worth noting: **#2264's fix is the one with the broadest reach and the smallest cost.** It doesn't fix any clobbering — it makes every clobber visible instead of silent, whatever caused it. That matches what the reporter actually asked for: *"This is about the diagnostic being wrong afterwards, whatever caused it."*

content.text:
Tested both. Direct answers:

## Does it match the right hook?

Yes — verified by spying on the actual dispatch through Lefthook:

```
entire hooks git prepare-commit-msg .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG message
entire hooks git commit-msg         .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG
entire hooks git post-commit
entire hooks git post-rewrite       amend
entire hooks git pre-push           origin https://example.test/r.git
```

All five reach the matching handler with git's own arguments intact, including pre-push's remote + URL.

## Does it resolve itself from errors?

Mostly — **three of four cases self-heal on the next agent turn**, one doesn't:

| Broken | Status reports | After one turn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `entire-lefthook.yml` deleted | degraded | **healed** |
| `extends` entry removed | degraded | **healed** |
| a script deleted | degraded | **healed** |
| **a script corrupted** | degraded | **still degraded** |

And the fourth doesn't recover via `doctor` either:

```
Error: git hook check failed: failed to reinstall git hooks:
lefthook entire.sh entry is not owned by Entire:
script path .lefthook-local/pre-push/entire.sh already exists
```

**Why:** install refuses to overwrite any script without Entire's ownership marker. A corrupted script has lost its marker, so it's indistinguishable from a file someone else put there — and the guard that protects a user's own script also traps Entire's own damaged one. It's stuck until someone deletes the file by hand.

That guard is right in principle; the gap is that there's no path out. It's **visible rather than silent** — status and doctor both report degraded, and native hooks keep delivering meanwhile, so no checkpoints are lost. But "run `entire doctor`" is what status tells you, and doctor then errors.

Two ways to close it, both small:
1. **Make doctor's message actionable** — name the file and say to remove it. ~5 lines, no behaviour change.
2. **Let `doctor --force` overwrite an unowned script at Entire's exact path**, since `--force` is already the "I mean it" escape hatch. Slightly more, and needs care not to weaken the guard on the normal path.

I'd do (1) now and leave (2), since it's a decision about how much `--force` is allowed to override. Worth noting this is the same trap the old code had — the ownership guard predates this PR — but the new mechanism has more artifacts that can be corrupted, so it's more reachable now.

Want me to add the actionable message?

content.text:
No — it doesn't fix everything. Three gaps, all confirmed just now.

## What it does fix

| From the tickets | |
| --- | --- |
| Lefthook reclaims `pre-push` on config change / npm install (#1349) | ✅ nothing of Entire's left to reclaim |
| `entire status` reports sync while hooks are missing (#2264) | ✅ reports blocked/degraded/ready |
| Lefthook classified as not-overwriting (#2263) | ✅ now `true` |
| `entire enable` re-wraps blindly with no detection (#1349) | ✅ detects and integrates instead |
| Routing and self-healing | ✅ all five hooks correct; 3 of 4 break-cases heal |

## What it doesn't

**1. The advice is still false.** `entire enable` printed, *after* installing the permanent integration:

> *"If Lefthook reinstalls hooks, run `entire enable` to restore Entire's hooks."*

Lefthook reinstalling is now harmless, and there's nothing to restore. #2263's actual complaint was the message, and flipping the flag upgraded "Note:" to "Warning:" while leaving the text wrong. I flagged this earlier as a task and never did it.

**2. Leftovers from the broken state aren't cleaned up.** Simulating a repo that already hit #1349 — `pre-push.old` and `pre-push.pre-entire` present — then enabling:

```
LEFTOVER: pre-push.old
LEFTOVER: pre-push.pre-entire
```

Both survive. `pre-push.old` is Lefthook's own backup, and its existence is what causes #1349's step 4 — the recurring `could not replace the hook: can't rename pre-push to pre-push.old - file already exists` error. **That error keeps firing after this fix.** Every existing affected repo is in exactly this state, so it's the upgrade path that matters most.

**3. A corrupted script can't recover** — the ownership guard traps Entire's own damaged file, and `doctor --force` errors out rather than fixing it.

## Also unverified

#1349 lists two more that I haven't tested: `entire configure --force` reinstalling the wrapper even with `push_sessions: false`, and `entire hooks git pre-push` being gated by `push_sessions` so a manager-invoked script no-ops. Under the new mechanism the script *is* manager-invoked, so the second one could mean checkpoints silently don't push when `push_sessions` is off — which may be correct, but I haven't checked.

Gaps 1 and 2 are small and belong in this PR — the false advice is ~10 lines, and clearing stale `.old`/`.pre-entire` backups when switching to Lefthook mode is maybe 20. Gap 3 and the `push_sessions` question I'd want your call on.

Want me to fix 1 and 2 and test the `push_sessions` interaction?

content.text:
No — and the comparison shows a real inconsistency I'd missed.

**Native repo:**

| Break | State | Heals? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| hook deleted | `absent` | ✅ |
| hook corrupted, marker gone | `absent` | ✅ **recovers** |
| hook edited, marker kept | `outdated` | ❌ deliberate — `c9604079` protects hand edits |

**Lefthook repo:**

| Break | State | Heals? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| script deleted | degraded | ✅ |
| script corrupted, marker gone | degraded | ❌ **does not recover** |

So the two paths classify the markerless case identically — "this file isn't ours" — and then do **opposite things**:

- **Native** backs the foreign file up to `.pre-entire` and writes Entire's hook. Recovers.
- **Lefthook** returns `ErrLefthookOwnedEntryConflict` and gives up. Stuck.

The only case that legitimately doesn't heal is the third native one, where the Entire marker survives and the body was edited — that's the deliberate protection, and status reports `outdated` rather than pretending.

So my earlier framing was wrong: it isn't "corrupted files can't be distinguished from foreign ones, so we refuse." Native already made the call that a markerless file at Entire's path gets backed up and replaced, and that's been shipping. Lefthook's stricter behaviour is an inconsistency, not a considered position.

**The fix is to make them match**: back up the unowned script to `entire.sh.pre-entire` and write ours, exactly as `InstallGitHook` does for `.git/hooks/*`. The user's file is preserved, the trap disappears, and both paths behave the same way for the same classification. Maybe 15 lines.

The one thing it changes: someone who deliberately put their own `entire.sh` in `.lefthook-local/<hook>/` would find it moved aside rather than getting an error. That's precisely what native does today for a foreign `.git/hooks/pre-push`, so it's consistent — but it is a behaviour change worth naming.

**Draft.** Replaces the implementation in #2343, which bundled this with an unrelated session-listing change (now #2363).

## Problem

In a repo that also uses Lefthook, Lefthook reclaims Entire's Git hooks and checkpoint capture stops silently. The trigger is routine: any `lefthook.yml` edit — including pulling a teammate's — or any `npm install`, via Lefthook's postinstall running `install -f`.

It is not a narrow window. Lefthook's installed hooks self-sync **on every run**, so the reclaim happens at the top of the very `pre-commit` the agent's own commit triggers — after Entire's turn-start repair has already run. Entire's existing self-heal cannot win that race. Meanwhile `entire status` reports "Checkpoints sync to: origin" (#2264) and `entire doctor` reports "NOT INSTALLED" — the two disagree.

## Approach

Entire owns `entire-lefthook.yml` outright and adds **one** `extends` entry to the clone-local config. Lefthook resolves `extends` at run time, so an already-installed launcher dispatches to Entire immediately — no `lefthook install`, no user action. Entire writes nothing into `.git/hooks/*`, so there is nothing left to reclaim.

Verified end to end against the real lefthook **2.1.10** binary, including with a **`lefthook.toml`** main config — a layout the previous mechanism refused outright.

## Why only Lefthook

I tested the other managers the same way. **pre-commit, Overcommit and hk all overwrite Entire's hooks at install time** — and all three are currently classified as not overwriting, which is fixed here. But none of them reclaims a *different* hook during a later commit. Only Lefthook does, which is why only Lefthook defeats the self-heal and justifies a config-level integration. #1250's general backend is not built: there is now evidence rather than a guess that a second adapter is not imminent.

## What this fixes beyond the headline

- **The recurring Lefthook error.** A repo that already hit #1349 carries `pre-push.old`; Lefthook then refuses to move the hook aside and errors on *every* sync. That outlives the integration unless the leftovers are cleared, which they now are — each only when its contents prove whose it was.
- **The advice was still false.** `entire enable` told users to re-run it after every Lefthook refresh, printed immediately after installing the integration that makes refreshes harmless. That message is what #2263 was filed about.
- **Corrupted scripts were unrecoverable.** Corruption destroys the ownership marker, so the script read as foreign and nothing could repair it — not a turn, not `doctor --force`. The native path had already settled this by backing up and replacing; the two now behave the same.
- **Ownership of `entire-lefthook.yml`.** The path is Entire's choice, the repository is the user's. A file there Entire did not write is displaced to `.pre-entire`, never destroyed.

## What was removed from #2343

- **Byte-exact matching of Lefthook's generated wrapper.** It pinned every package-manager probe branch, so the next Lefthook release would read as a foreign hook and Entire would write native wrappers over Lefthook's own — #1349 in reverse. Its sibling matched strings byte-identical to this repo's own test fixtures, so no test exercised the branch real Lefthook takes.
- **A second, nested rollback layer**, inside a snapshot that already covered the same paths plus the native hooks and backups.
- **The merge into the user's `lefthook-local.yml`**, and with it `validateLefthookMainConfig`, the main-config-derived rejections, and eight near-identical `yaml.Node` traversals. `lefthook_yaml.go` is gone.
- **Proactive turn-start warnings** (~950 lines) — that is #1965's feature, not this one.

## Size

2,145 production / 2,841 test / 155 docs+e2e. Production is down from 3,156 in #2343. The test ratio is 1.32, below the `strategy` package's own 1.71.

## Known issue, not introduced here

The generated pre-push script passes `"$2"` unconditionally, so hooks written by this version fail against an older `entire` on `PATH` (`accepts 1 arg(s), received 2`). The ABI widening came from #2343; flagging it as a real mixed-version hazard.

## Still to do

Rebase onto current main.

Closes #2264, #1349, #2263. Does **not** close #2237 — that backup-chain path is untouched here.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

content.text:
Merge done and pushed. Answering your three questions.

## Is the plan to close #2343?

Yes — **#2365 replaces it entirely.** Everything in #2343 is either in #2365, moved to #2363 (session listing), or deliberately deferred to #1965 (proactive warnings). Nothing is lost. I haven't closed it because that's yours to do, and the plan was to keep it as the reference until the replacement is verified. It's verified now.

## The title is misleading

Agreed, and that's been the root of a lot of this. #2343 is called *"fix: make checkpoint status reflect hook health"* — named after a few hundred lines of the 6,807. The substance was always the Lefthook durability fix. #2365 is titled `fix(hooks): keep checkpoint delivery working when Lefthook reclaims hooks`, which is what it does.

## The split

I hadn't been thinking about it — I was in the merge. But the merge changed the answer, so here's a real one:

**#2337 landing made the status half much smaller.** It now owns `computeCheckpointSyncInfo`, `resolveDedicatedReadSource`, and all the read-source/push-disabled rendering. Our status contribution is down to the snapshot, the hook-health lines, and three JSON fields — roughly **120 production lines**, not the 215 I quoted before.

That makes a split cleaner than it was:

| | Production | Closes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A** — status reports hook health + the health API + native inspection | ~600 | **#2264, #2263** |
| **B** — Lefthook integration | ~1,500 | **#1349** |

B still depends on A for `CheckGitHookIntegration`, so it's sequential. And A is only genuinely small if the health API goes with it — which it must, since status calls it.

**Two things about the merge worth flagging**, both of which cost real time:

- `dedicated_rejected_by_fetch_owner` **fails on `origin/main` itself**, both backends. Pre-existing from #2337, not mine. I chased it for a while before thinking to check the baseline.
- Where the branches disagreed, I gave #2337 the sync semantics and this branch the hook health. The one genuine conflict: #2337's tests assert a sync destination in repos with *no hooks installed*. Rather than suppress the whole block, blocked now relabels `Checkpoints sync to:` → `Configured destination:`, which kills the #2264 false promise but keeps #2337's diagnostics visible.

Current: **5,135** (2,116 production / 2,864 tests / 155 docs).

Want me to do the A/B split, or leave it as one and have you close #2343?

| | Production | Tests | **Total** | Closes |

| **A** — inspect and report hook health | 913 | ~2,055 | **~2,950** | #2264, #2263 |

Two ~3,000-line PRs instead of one 5,135.

**Why this seam and not the one I proposed an hour ago:** A includes the *read* side of Lefthook — detection, artifact inspection, the health API — so `checkGitHookIntegrationInDir` compiles as-is. My earlier "A = everyone-affecting" split would have forced a native-only health API in A that B then rewrites, which is churn. This one moves whole files.

What each does on its own:

- **A**: `entire status` and `doctor` report the truth for every repo including Lefthook ones — `git_hooks`, `checkpoint_sync_state`, correct manager classification and advice. It does **not** install the integration, so Lefthook still clobbers; status just stops lying about it. That's #2264 as its reporter actually scoped it: *"the diagnostic being wrong afterwards, whatever caused it."*
- **B**: adds the install/repair/remove path so the clobbering stops.

**B depends on A** (it calls `CheckGitHookIntegration`), so B branches from A and targets it; GitHub retargets B to main automatically when A merges.

One caveat worth stating: A's ~2,055 test lines include the health-state matrix, which is most of `hook_integration_test.go`. My allocation of that file (450/443) is the softest number here — it could shift a few hundred either way.

Want me to build the two branches? And on #2343 — I'll close it once both are open and green, with a comment pointing at the three replacements (#2363, A, B), unless you'd rather do it yourself.

You're right, and I've been doing the wrong thing — packaging #2343's architecture instead of asking whether it's needed.

Here's what's actually wrong with Lefthook, stated plainly:

**Lefthook owns `.git/hooks/*` and regenerates them from its config on every run. Entire wants to be in those files. Two tools, one file.** The fix is that Entire stops wanting the file and registers with Lefthook instead.

I proved what that takes with my own prototype, before writing any production code:

```yaml
entire-lefthook.yml        12 lines, generated
lefthook-local.yml          1 extends line
.lefthook-local/<hook>/entire.sh    3 lines each
```

That's the whole mechanism. The code to produce and check it:

| | ~Lines |
| --- | --- |
| Render Entire's config | 15 |
| Render the scripts (reuses `buildHookSpecs`) | 15 |
| Write them atomically (reuses `jsonutil.WriteFileAtomicIn`) | 30 |
| Add one `extends` entry to the local config | 60 |
| Find which local config Lefthook reads | 30 |
| Inspect: are they ours and current | 50 |
| Remove on uninstall | 40 |
| Clear the stale `.old` backup that makes Lefthook error forever | 40 |
| Wire into enable / doctor / status | 40 |
| **Production** | **~320** |

With tests at this repo's ratio: **~850 total.**

**So why is the PR 2,116 production lines?** Because #2343 built infrastructure around the fix, and I preserved it:

- a five-state health API with modes and reason codes — 217
- a coordinator with snapshot/rollback, two delivery bridges, its own hooks-root resolution — 635
- widening the *native* hook inspection — 171
- status rendering — 120

None of that is required to stop Lefthook clobbering Entire. The health API exists because the coordinator needed to describe itself; the coordinator exists because it manages two mechanisms at once; the native widening came along for the ride.

**What I'd do: write the minimal fix against main and abandon the diff-splitting.** ~850 lines, one PR, closes #1349 and #2263. Status reporting (#2264) goes with it using main's existing three-state check, as its reporter actually specified — that's maybe another 80 lines, not 120 plus a new API.

I'd keep from this work: the `extends` mechanism itself (verified against the real binary), the stale-backup cleanup, the ownership guards on Entire's own files, and the structural Lefthook-launcher predicate. Those are findings, not architecture.

Want me to build that? It's a rewrite, not a re-package — which is why nothing I proposed for the last several rounds got the number down.

44		lefthookScriptDir = ".lefthook-local"
45		lefthookScript    = "entire.sh"
46		// lefthookOwnedMarker identifies a file as Entire's. Removal and
47		// overwriting both require it: the path is Entire's choice, but the
48		// repository is the user's.
49		lefthookOwnedMarker = "entire-cli-owned:lefthook:v1"
50	)
51	
52	// ErrLefthookLocalConfigUnwritable reports a local config Entire will not
53	// edit. Lefthook reads exactly one local config and lefthook-local.yml takes
54	// precedence over lefthook-local.toml, so creating the former beside a user's
55	// latter would silently stop their hooks running. Entire declines instead and
56	// leaves its native hooks in place.
57	var ErrLefthookLocalConfigUnwritable = errors.New("lefthook local config is not YAML")
58	
59	// lefthookLocalConfigNames are the local config names Lefthook reads, in its
60	// own precedence order. Writing into anything but the first match present
61	// would be a silent no-op.
62	var lefthookLocalConfigNames = []string{
63		"lefthook-local.yml", "lefthook-local.yaml",
64		"lefthook-local.json", "lefthook-local.toml",
65		".lefthook-local.yml", ".lefthook-local.yaml",
66		".lefthook-local.json", ".lefthook-local.toml",
67	}
68	
69	// LefthookManaged reports whether this repository is managed by Lefthook.
70	func LefthookManaged(repoRoot string) bool {
71		for _, m := range detectHookManagers(repoRoot) {
72			if m.Name == "Lefthook" {
73				return true
74			}
75		}
76		return false
77	}
78	
79	// EnsureLefthookIntegration registers Entire with Lefthook, returning the
80	// number of artifacts written.
81	//
82	// There is deliberately no rollback. Every write is atomic and content-
83	// idempotent, and the entry that activates the integration is written last, so
84	// a failure part way through leaves inert files that the next install
85	// overwrites. EnsureSetup runs at every turn start, so "the next install" is a
86	// guarantee rather than a hope.
87	func EnsureLefthookIntegration(ctx context.Context, absolutePath bool) (int, error) {
88		repoRoot, err := paths.WorktreeRoot(ctx)
89		if err != nil {
90			return 0, fmt.Errorf("resolve worktree root: %w", err)
91		}
92		root, err := worktreedir.OpenAt(repoRoot)
93		if err != nil {
94			return 0, fmt.Errorf("open worktree: %w", err)
95		}
96		cmdPrefix, err := hookCmdPrefix(absolutePath)
97		if err != nil {
98			return 0, err
99		}
100	
101		written := 0
102		for _, spec := range buildHookSpecs(cmdPrefix) {
103			name := lefthookScriptPath(spec.name)
104			if err := displaceUnowned(root, name, 0o755); err != nil {
105				return 0, err
106			}
107			if err := osroot.MkdirAllNoSymlink(root, filepath.ToSlash(filepath.Dir(name)), 0o755); err != nil {
108				return 0, fmt.Errorf("create %s: %w", filepath.Dir(name), err)
109			}
110			changed, writeErr := writeHookFile(root, name, renderLefthookScript(spec))
111			if writeErr != nil {
112				return 0, writeErr
113			}
114			if changed {
115				written++
116			}
117		}
118	
119		if err := displaceUnowned(root, entireLefthookConfig, 0o644); err != nil {
120			return 0, err
121		}
122		changed, err := writeOwnedConfig(root)
123		if err != nil {
124			return 0, err
125		}
126		if changed {
127			written++
128		}
129	
130		// Last: this is what makes Lefthook load any of the above.
131		if _, err := ensureExtendsEntry(root); err != nil {
132			return 0, err
133		}
134		if err := clearStaleBackups(ctx, repoRoot); err != nil {
135			return 0, err
136		}
137		return written, nil
138	}
139	
140	// LefthookIntegrationCurrent reports whether Entire's artifacts are present
141	// and current: its config, the extends entry pointing at it, and every script.
142	func LefthookIntegrationCurrent(ctx context.Context, absolutePath bool) (bool, error) {
143		repoRoot, err := paths.WorktreeRoot(ctx)
144		if err != nil {
145			return false, fmt.Errorf("resolve worktree root: %w", err)
146		}
147		root, err := worktreedir.OpenAt(repoRoot)
148		if err != nil {
149			return false, fmt.Errorf("open worktree: %w", err)
150		}
151		want, err := renderOwnedConfig()
152		if err != nil {
153			return false, err
154		}
155		data, err := osroot.ReadFileNoFollow(root, entireLefthookConfig)
156		if err != nil || string(data) != want {
157			return false, nil //nolint:nilerr // a missing or stale config is "not current", not a failure
158		}
159		present, err := extendsEntryPresent(root)

161			return false, err
162		}
163		cmdPrefix, err := hookCmdPrefix(absolutePath)
164		if err != nil {
165			return false, err
166		}
167		for _, spec := range buildHookSpecs(cmdPrefix) {

170				return false, nil //nolint:nilerr // same: stale, not broken
171			}
172		}
173		return true, nil
174	}

178	func RemoveLefthookIntegration(ctx context.Context) (int, error) {

201			}
202			removed++
203		}
204		dropped, err := removeExtendsEntry(root)
205		if err != nil {
206			return removed, err
207		}
208		if dropped {
209			removed++
210		}
211		return removed, nil
212	}

package strategy

import (
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/paths"
	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/testutil"
	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
)

// newLefthookRepo is an isolated repository that looks Lefthook-managed.
func newLefthookRepo(t *testing.T, mainConfig string) string {
	t.Helper()
	dir := t.TempDir()
	testutil.InitRepo(t, dir)
	name, body := "lefthook.yml", "pre-commit: {}\n"
	if mainConfig != "" {
		name, body = mainConfig, "pre-commit: {}\n"
	}
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(dir, name), []byte(body), 0o644))
	t.Chdir(dir)
	paths.ClearWorktreeRootCache()
	t.Cleanup(paths.ClearWorktreeRootCache)
	return dir
}

// Install writes Entire's own config, one extends entry, and a script per
// hook — and nothing into Lefthook's own config.
func TestEnsureLefthookIntegration(t *testing.T) {
	dir := newLefthookRepo(t, "")
	mainBefore, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, "lefthook.yml"))
	require.NoError(t, err)

	written, err := EnsureLefthookIntegration(t.Context(), false)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Positive(t, written)

	owned, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, entireLefthookConfig))
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Contains(t, string(owned), lefthookOwnedMarker)
	require.Contains(t, string(owned), "source_dir_local: "+lefthookScriptDir)

	local, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, "lefthook-local.yml"))
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Contains(t, string(local), entireLefthookConfig)
	require.Equal(t, 1, strings.Count(string(local), entireLefthookConfig))

	for _, hook := range gitHookNames {
		script, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, lefthookScriptPath(hook)))
		require.NoError(t, err, hook)
		require.Contains(t, string(script), lefthookOwnedMarker, hook)
		require.Contains(t, string(script), "hooks git "+hook, hook)
		info, err := os.Stat(filepath.Join(dir, lefthookScriptPath(hook)))
		require.NoError(t, err)
		require.NotZero(t, info.Mode().Perm()&0o111, "%s must be executable", hook)
	}

	mainAfter, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, "lefthook.yml"))
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Equal(t, mainBefore, mainAfter, "Lefthook's own config must not be touched")

	current, err := LefthookIntegrationCurrent(t.Context(), false)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.True(t, current)

	// Repeat installs are no-ops.
	written, err = EnsureLefthookIntegration(t.Context(), false)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Zero(t, written)
}

// Entire never reads Lefthook's main config, so its format and location are
// irrelevant — .toml and .config/ repos work like any other.
func TestEnsureLefthookIntegration_MainConfigFormatIsIrrelevant(t *testing.T) {
	for _, name := range []string{"lefthook.toml", "lefthook.json", ".lefthook.yaml"} {
		t.Run(name, func(t *testing.T) {
			newLefthookRepo(t, name)
			_, err := EnsureLefthookIntegration(t.Context(), false)
			require.NoError(t, err)
			current, err := LefthookIntegrationCurrent(t.Context(), false)
			require.NoError(t, err)
			require.True(t, current)
		})
	}
}

// The extends entry goes into the user's local config without disturbing it.
func TestEnsureLefthookIntegration_PreservesLocalConfig(t *testing.T) {
	for _, tc := range []struct{ name, local string; want []string }{

package strategy

import (
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/paths"
	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/testutil"
	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
)

// newLefthookRepo is an isolated repository that looks Lefthook-managed.
func newLefthookRepo(t *testing.T, mainConfig string) string {
	t.Helper()
	dir := t.TempDir()
	testutil.InitRepo(t, dir)
	name, body := "lefthook.yml", "pre-commit: {}\n"
	if mainConfig != "" {
		name, body = mainConfig, "pre-commit: {}\n"
	}
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(dir, name), []byte(body), 0o644))
	t.Chdir(dir)
	paths.ClearWorktreeRootCache()
	t.Cleanup(paths.ClearWorktreeRootCache)
	return dir
}

// Install writes Entire's own config, one extends entry, and a script per
// hook — and nothing into Lefthook's own config.
func TestEnsureLefthookIntegration(t *testing.T) {
	dir := newLefthookRepo(t, "")
	mainBefore, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, "lefthook.yml"))
	require.NoError(t, err)

	written, err := EnsureLefthookIntegration(t.Context(), false)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Positive(t, written)

	owned, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, entireLefthookConfig))
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Contains(t, string(owned), lefthookOwnedMarker)
	require.Contains(t, string(owned), "source_dir_local: "+lefthookScriptDir)

	local, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, "lefthook-local.yml"))
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Contains(t, string(local), entireLefthookConfig)
	require.Equal(t, 1, strings.Count(string(local), entireLefthookConfig))

	for _, hook := range gitHookNames {
		script, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, lefthookScriptPath(hook)))
		require.NoError(t, err, hook)
		require.Contains(t, string(script), lefthookOwnedMarker, hook)
		require.Contains(t, string(script), "hooks git "+hook, hook)
		info, err := os.Stat(filepath.Join(dir, lefthookScriptPath(hook)))
		require.NoError(t, err)
		require.NotZero(t, info.Mode().Perm()&0o111, "%s must be executable", hook)
	}

	mainAfter, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, "lefthook.yml"))
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Equal(t, mainBefore, mainAfter, "Lefthook's own config must not be touched")

	current, err := LefthookIntegrationCurrent(t.Context(), false)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.True(t, current)

	// Repeat installs are no-ops.
	written, err = EnsureLefthookIntegration(t.Context(), false)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Zero(t, written)
}

// Entire never reads Lefthook's main config, so its format and location are
// irrelevant — .toml and .config/ repos work like any other.
func TestEnsureLefthookIntegration_MainConfigFormatIsIrrelevant(t *testing.T) {
	for _, name := range []string{"lefthook.toml", "lefthook.json", ".lefthook.yaml"} {
		t.Run(name, func(t *testing.T) {
			newLefthookRepo(t, name)
			_, err := EnsureLefthookIntegration(t.Context(), false)
			require.NoError(t, err)
			current, err := LefthookIntegrationCurrent(t.Context(), false)
			require.NoError(t, err)
			require.True(t, current)
		})
	}
}

// The extends entry goes into the user's local config without disturbing it.
func TestEnsureLefthookIntegration_PreservesLocalConfig(t *testing.T) {
	for _, tc := range []struct{ name, local string; want []string }{
		{"existing content", "# keep me\npre-commit:\n  commands:\n    mine:\n      run: true\n",
			[]string{"# keep me", "mine"}},
		{"existing extends", "extends:\n  - user.yml\n", []string{"user.yml"}},
	} {
		t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
			dir := newLefthookRepo(t, "")
			require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(dir, "lefthook-local.yml"), []byte(tc.local), 0o644))
			_, err := EnsureLefthookIntegration(t.Context(), false)
			require.NoError(t, err)

			got, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, "lefthook-local.yml"))
			require.NoError(t, err)
			require.Contains(t, string(got), entireLefthookConfig)
			for _, want := range tc.want {
				require.Contains(t, string(got), want)
			}
		})
	}
}

// lefthook-local.yml takes precedence over lefthook-local.toml, so creating
// the former beside a user's latter would silently stop their hooks running.
func REDACTED(t *testing.T) {
	dir := newLefthookRepo(t, "")
	tomlPath := filepath.Join(dir, "lefthook-local.toml")
	original := []byte("[pre-commit.commands.mine]\nrun = \"true\"\n")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(tomlPath, original, 0o644))

	_, err := EnsureLefthookIntegration(t.Context(), false)
	require.ErrorIs(t, err, ErrLefthookLocalConfigUnwritable)

	after, err := os.ReadFile(tomlPath)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Equal(t, original, after)
	_, statErr := os.Stat(filepath.Join(dir, "lefthook-local.yml"))
	require.True(t, os.IsNotExist(statErr), "must not create a shadowing lefthook-local.yml")
}

// A file Entire did not write is displaced, never destroyed. Corruption
// destroys the marker, so a damaged script would otherwise read as foreign and
// could never be repaired.
func TestEnsureLefthookIntegration_DisplacesUnownedFiles(t *testing.T) {
	dir := newLefthookRepo(t, "")
	scriptPath := filepath.Join(dir, lefthookScriptPath("pre-push"))
	require.NoError(t, os.MkdirAll(filepath.Dir(scriptPath), 0o755))
	theirs := []byte("#!/bin/sh\necho mine\n")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(scriptPath, theirs, 0o755))
	configPath := filepath.Join(dir, entireLefthookConfig)
	theirConfig := []byte("# not Entire's\nkey: value\n")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(configPath, theirConfig, 0o644))

	_, err := EnsureLefthookIntegration(t.Context(), false)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	backup, err := os.ReadFile(scriptPath + GitHookBackupSuffix)
	require.NoError(t, err, "the displaced script must be kept")
	require.Equal(t, theirs, backup)
	backup, err = os.ReadFile(configPath + GitHookBackupSuffix)
	require.NoError(t, err, "the displaced config must be kept")
	require.Equal(t, theirConfig, backup)

	current, err := LefthookIntegrationCurrent(t.Context(), false)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.True(t, current, "and Entire's own artifacts installed over them")
}

// Uninstall takes only what Entire wrote.
func TestRemoveLefthookIntegration(t *testing.T) {
	dir := newLefthookRepo(t, "")
	localPath := filepath.Join(dir, "lefthook-local.yml")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(localPath, []byte("pre-commit:\n  commands:\n    mine:\n      run: true\n"), 0o644))
	_, err := EnsureLefthookIntegration(t.Context(), false)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	removed, err := RemoveLefthookIntegration(t.Context())
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Positive(t, removed)

	_, statErr := os.Stat(filepath.Join(dir, entireLefthookConfig))
	require.True(t, os.IsNotExist(statErr))
	local, err := os.ReadFile(localPath)
	require.NoError(t, err, "the user's local config must survive")
	require.NotContains(t, string(local), entireLefthookConfig)
	require.Contains(t, string(local), "mine")

	current, err := LefthookIntegrationCurrent(t.Context(), false)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.False(t, current)
}

// A foreign file at Entire's config path is not Entire's to delete.
func TestRemoveLefthookIntegration_LeavesForeignFiles(t *testing.T) {
	dir := newLefthookRepo(t, "")
	configPath := filepath.Join(dir, entireLefthookConfig)
	theirs := []byte("# not Entire's\nkey: value\n")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(configPath, theirs, 0o644))

	_, err := RemoveLefthookIntegration(t.Context())
	require.NoError(t, err)
	after, err := os.ReadFile(configPath)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Equal(t, theirs, after)
}

// A repo that already hit #1349 carries <hook>.old, and Lefthook then errors
// on every sync until it is gone. Clearing it is part of the fix.
func TestEnsureLefthookIntegration_ClearsStaleBackups(t *testing.T) {
	dir := newLefthookRepo(t, "")
	hooksDir := filepath.Join(dir, ".git", "hooks")
	require.NoError(t, os.MkdirAll(hooksDir, 0o755))
	stale := filepath.Join(hooksDir, "pre-push.old")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(stale,
		[]byte("#!/bin/sh\n# "+entireHookMarker+"\nentire hooks git pre-push \"$1\"\n"), 0o755))
	// A backup that is not ours stays put.
	keep := filepath.Join(hooksDir, "commit-msg.old")
	theirs := []byte("#!/bin/sh\necho someone else\n")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(keep, theirs, 0o755))

	_, err := EnsureLefthookIntegration(t.Context(), false)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	_, statErr := os.Stat(stale)
	require.True(t, os.IsNotExist(statErr), "Entire's stale wrapper backup must be cleared")
	after, err := os.ReadFile(keep)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Equal(t, theirs, after, "another tool's backup must be left alone")
}

// Delivery is judged on the integration in a Lefthook repo, because Lefthook
// owns .git/hooks/* and rewrites them constantly.
func TestCheckHookDelivery_Lefthook(t *testing.T) {
	newLefthookRepo(t, "")
	got := CheckHookDelivery(t.Context(), false)
	require.False(t, got.OK, "not registered yet")
	require.Equal(t, "Lefthook", got.Manager)
	require.NotEmpty(t, got.Reason)

	_, err := EnsureLefthookIntegration(t.Context(), false)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	got = CheckHookDelivery(t.Context(), false)
	require.True(t, got.OK)
	require.Equal(t, "Lefthook", got.Manager)
	require.Empty(t, got.Reason)
}

// In a repo with no hook manager, delivery is the native hook state.
func TestCheckHookDelivery_Native(t *testing.T) {
	dir := t.TempDir()
	testutil.InitRepo(t, dir)
	t.Chdir(dir)
	paths.ClearWorktreeRootCache()
	t.Cleanup(paths.ClearWorktreeRootCache)
	ClearHooksDirCache()

	got := CheckHookDelivery(t.Context(), false)
	require.False(t, got.OK)
	require.Empty(t, got.Manager)

	if _, err := ReinstallGitHooks(t.Context()); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("ReinstallGitHooks: %v", err)
	}
	ClearHooksDirCache()
	got = CheckHookDelivery(t.Context(), false)
	require.True(t, got.OK)
	require.Empty(t, got.Manager)
}

name: over-writing-tests
description: "Peyton's feedback that I write too many tests; prefer one table-driven test over several near-identical ones"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory

I tend to over-produce tests — e.g. proposing five separate tests for one
function when one table-driven test covers the same cases, or an 11-row
validation table where 6 rows cover every distinct class. Peyton called this
out on 2026-09-10 while reviewing the PR #2343 rework plan.

**Why:** test volume is review burden too. Near-identical test bodies that
differ by one fixture value cost the same to read as genuinely distinct cases
but carry none of the extra signal, and they make the real coverage harder to
see. This repo's own ratio is ~1.7 test:production lines in
`cmd/entire/cli/strategy`, so the bar is not "more tests" — it's distinct
failure modes.

**How to apply:** before proposing a set of tests, collapse them by failure
class — one table-driven test per class, not one test per input. Prefer a
single JSON-contract assertion over many rendered-text assertions, which are
brittle and low-value. When a plan lists N new tests for one function, that is
the signal to re-check. Exception worth keeping: code that can destroy user
data (hook rewriting, file ownership, symlink traversal) earns its dedicated
cases — see [[diagnose-then-decide-together]] for the related habit of
reporting options instead of expanding scope unasked.
